6b(1).fact: Scouting America guidance affirms that any real experience of feeling separated from peers provides valid material for thoughtful discussion and growth.
6b(1).misconception: Scouts must share a traumatic crisis or severe bullying event rather than an everyday occurrence like being excluded from a team or game.
6b(1).pamphlet_summary: Scouts discuss a personal encounter with exclusion alongside a peer with a different identity, examining the emotional impact and whether anyone intervened. The discussion asks youth to reflect on lessons learned and consider how they would handle similar situations today (p. 8).
6b(1).socratic_question: When you think back to a time you felt left out of a group, what specific action from someone nearby would have helped you feel supported?

6b(2).fact: Scouting America provides the hypothetical scenario as an equal option so any youth can explore exclusion dynamics without feeling compelled to disclose private personal experiences.
6b(2).misconception: Scouts may only choose the hypothetical scenario if they have never experienced exclusion in their personal lives.
6b(2).pamphlet_summary: Scouts analyze a scenario involving a newcomer rejected at two school lunch tables to evaluate the feelings and peer dynamics of social isolation. This alternative allows youth to consider how bystanders could have acted differently and how they can actively welcome new students in their own schools (p. 9).
6b(2).socratic_question: What small gesture could an observant student make in that cafeteria to turn an uncomfortable rejection into a welcoming experience?
